title: Konrad Bloch, a Jewish refugee from Germany, discovered how the body builds cholesterol and won the Nobel Prize in Medicine

trailer.text: Konrad Bloch, who won the 1964 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine together with Feodor Lynen, was born in 1912 in Neisse to Jewish parents.
The Nazi authorities ordered him to end his chemistry studies in Munich, and he had to flee.
In 1936 he was able to immigrate to the United States.
In 1942 he began studying with David Rittenberg how the body makes cholesterol, and worked on it for almost twenty years.
He was awarded the prize "for their discoveries concerning the mechanism and regulation of the cholesterol and fatty acid metabolism".

stations.title: A Jewish child in Neisse, a student in Munich

paragraphs.text: Konrad Bloch was born on 21 January 1912 in Neisse, Upper Silesia, then in Germany.
His parents were Fritz Bloch and Hedwig, née Striemer.
His parents were Jewish.
He studied chemistry in Munich.
According to the National Academy of Sciences memoir, Nazism had already spread to the university by then, and Jews were denied all manner of advancement.
According to the obituary in the Harvard Gazette, the Nazi authorities ordered him, in line with the new racial laws, to end his studies.
According to TIME magazine, he was not allowed to continue his studies because he was a Jew.
In 1934 his studies ended for racial reasons, after he had obtained the degree of Diplom-Ingenieur in Chemistry.

At a time when Nazism had already spread to the university and Jews were denied any advancement, his thesis was deemed unsatisfactory, and he was denied admission to graduate studies at several of Germany's leading institutions.
Bloch left Germany and found a temporary position at a Swiss research institute in Davos.
There he investigated the phospholipids of tubercle bacilli.
It was his first exposure to biochemical research.
In 1936 his residential permit in Switzerland was about to expire, without any chance of renewal.
Then two letters arrived.
The first informed him that he had been appointed an assistant in biological chemistry at Yale Medical School.
The second said there was no salary for the position.
Bloch took the first letter to the U.S. consulate in Frankfurt, and that was enough to get him an immigration visa.
In 1936 he came to the United States, as he had long hoped.
With the support of the Wallerstein Foundation he entered the Department of Biochemistry at Columbia University, as a graduate student under Hans Clarke.
According to the National Academy memoir, his doctoral dissertation included some of the research he had done in Switzerland.
After the doctorate, Rudolf Schoenheimer asked Bloch to join his group.
Schoenheimer adventurously adopted a new method: heavy isotopes, to decipher biochemical pathways.
The researchers fed labeled compounds to rats, and then isolated what the body had made from them.

According to Encyclopedia.com, Schoenheimer and his associate David Rittenberg developed a method of using radioisotopes (radioactive forms of atoms) to track the path of particular molecules in cells and living organisms.
In 1941 Bloch married Lore Teutsch, a native of Munich, and they had two children, Peter and Susan.
According to TIME, he became an American citizen in 1944.
According to the Encyclopedia of World Biography, Bloch received his doctorate in biochemistry in 1938, at the Columbia University School of Medicine.

stations.title: The question: where does cholesterol come from?

paragraphs.text: According to Encyclopedia.com, before Bloch's research scientists knew little about cholesterol, although many believed it was connected to arteriosclerosis.

According to TIME, incomplete medical research first suggested that cholesterol was a root cause of much artery disease and many heart attacks, but after more complex studies the researchers said that cholesterol itself may not be particularly important.
TIME wrote that medical science needed to learn a great deal more about what cholesterol does, where it comes from and where it goes.
In 1942 Bloch, together with David Rittenberg, began studying how the body makes cholesterol.
This work occupied him for almost twenty years.

stations.title: From acetate to cholesterol, step by step

paragraphs.text: According to Britannica, in 1942 Bloch and Rittenberg discovered that acetic acid is the major building block of cholesterol.
Bloch was fascinated by how the two carbons of acetate build the scaffold of cholesterol.
According to Wikipedia, he traced all the carbon atoms in cholesterol back to acetate.
He grew rat-liver cells in the test tube, and saw that they make cholesterol from the much simpler acetate ion.
According to TIME, Bloch learned that most of the cholesterol in the bodies of animals and humans does not come from cholesterol in food.
According to TIME, the cholesterol "factories" are mainly in the liver, but many other cells in the body can make some of it.
According to Wikipedia, the work showed that the body first makes squalene from acetate over many steps, and then converts it to cholesterol.
According to Wikipedia, some of the research was done using radioactive acetate in bread mold, because fungi also produce squalene.
According to the National Academy memoir, a nighttime session with his colleague R. B. Woodward led to a proposal for how squalene closes into rings.
Bloch did the degradations and crystallizations himself to verify that the proposal was correct.
Step by step, molecule by molecule, his group proceeded along the pathway, and along the way converged with Lynen's group.
According to Britannica, Lynen and his collaborators in Munich, and Cornforth and Popják in England, also joined the research.
According to Wikipedia, Bloch discovered that bile and a female sex hormone are made from cholesterol, and so it emerged that all steroids are made from it.
According to Wikipedia, he was also one of several researchers who showed that acetyl Coenzyme A is turned into mevalonic acid.
According to the National Academy memoir, Bloch deciphered the chemical code and the molecular logic underlying steroids.
In 1946 Bloch moved to the University of Chicago as Assistant Professor of Biochemistry.
In 1953, as a Guggenheim fellow, he spent a year in Zurich with Ružička and Prelog and their colleagues.
In 1954 he was appointed Higgins Professor of Biochemistry at Harvard.
His stated reason for the move was that he wanted to raise his children in a less urban environment.
In 1968 he became Chairman of the Department.
According to the Encyclopedia of World Biography, Bloch became an associate professor at the University of Chicago in 1948 and a full professor in 1950.
The 1964 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded jointly to Konrad Bloch and Feodor Lynen.
The prize was awarded "for their discoveries concerning the mechanism and regulation of the cholesterol and fatty acid metabolism".
At the time of the award Bloch worked at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
According to TIME, two biochemists, an American and a German, shared a prize worth 53 thousand dollars.
According to the Nobel website, Bloch and Lynen and their groups investigated how cholesterol and fatty acids are formed and converted in the body.
According to the website, this knowledge is important for understanding heart disease and other illnesses in which changes in cholesterol formation can play a role.
According to the New York Times, as cited by Encyclopedia.com, Bloch refused to be photographed in front of a sign celebrating him at the time of the prize.

stations.title: What came after him, and the man himself

paragraphs.text: According to the National Academy memoir, Bloch's research paved the way for the research of Brown and Goldstein on disorders of cholesterol metabolism and heart disease.
Brown and Goldstein showed that dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism causes many forms of cardiovascular disease, and won the Nobel Prize for it in 1985.
According to Britannica, the discovery facilitated medical research on the relation of blood cholesterol levels to atherosclerosis.
According to the Crimson, Elias Corey said the discovery had a great effect on drug development, and was used widely in medicine to control cholesterol levels and diseases of the circulatory system.
Barry Bloom, dean of the School of Public Health, wrote that working out the pathway by which cholesterol is built was one of Bloch's important achievements.
According to him, it was one of the most challenging problems that biochemistry had tried to solve up to that point.
Dean Jeremy Knowles called him a marvelously perceptive biochemist and a wise, generous, and cultivated man who forged the connections between chemistry and biochemistry.
Bloch also received the Fritzsche Award, the Notre Dame Centennial Science Award and the Cardano Medal.
According to Wikipedia, in 1985 he became a Fellow of the Royal Society, and in 1988 he received the U.S. National Medal of Science.
He was remarkably humble about his talents and accomplishments.
According to Bloom, he was a scientific giant, but always a modest person, generous with his thoughts and his scientific materials.
In 1982, at age 70, he retired from full-time teaching, but remained active.
He wrote books, among them the essay collection "Blondes in Venetian Paintings, the Nine-Banded Armadillo, and Other Essays in Biochemistry" (1994).
Bloch died on Sunday, October 15, at the age of 88, at Lahey Clinic in Burlington, Massachusetts.

disagreements.question: How many steps make up the process that produces cholesterol?

versions.says: According to Britannica, thirty or more steps
Bloch told TIME: a sequence of approximately 36 biochemical reactions
Bloch said with a smile that it might turn out there are 39 reactions

claims.text: לפי טיים, שני ביוכימאים, אמריקאי וגרמני, חלקו את פרס נובל 1964, ששווה 53 אלף דולר.
claims.quote: two biochemists, an American and a German, last week shared the 1964 Nobel Prize (worth $53,000) in physiology and medicine.

claims.text: לפי אתר נובל, בלוך ולינן וקבוצותיהם חקרו כיצד נוצרים ומומרים כולסטרול וחומצות שומן בגוף.
claims.quote: Konrad Bloch and Feodor Lynen and their respective colleagues investigated how cholesterol and fatty acids are formed and converted in the body.

claims.text: אתר נובל: הידע חשוב להבנת מחלות לב ומחלות אחרות שבהן שינויים ביצירת כולסטרול עשויים למלא תפקיד.
claims.quote: This knowledge is important for an understanding of heart disease and other illnesses in which changes in cholesterol formation can play a role.

claims.text: לפי הניו יורק טיימס כפי שמצוטט, בלוך סירב להצטלם מול שלט שחגג אותו בעת הענקת הפרס.
claims.quote: When he was awarded the Nobel Prize, the New York Times reported that he refused to have his picture taken in front of a sign that read

claims.text: לפי ההספד של האקדמיה הלאומית, מחקרו של בלוך סלל את הדרך למחקרם של בראון וגולדשטיין על הפרעות בחילוף הכולסטרול ומחלות לב וכלי דם.
claims.quote: Bloch’s decision to unravel how cholesterol is made was fruitful in another sense, because it paved the way for subsequent studies by Michael S. Brown and Joseph L. Goldstein

claims.text: בראון וגולדשטיין הראו שהפרעה בחילוף הכולסטרול גורמת לצורות רבות של מחלות לב וכלי דם, ובשל כך זכו בנובל ב-1985.
claims.quote: showing that dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism is causative in many forms of cardiovascular diseases, which garnered them the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1985.

claims.text: לפי בריטניקה, התגלית הקלה על מחקר רפואי בקשר בין רמות כולסטרול בדם לטרשת עורקים.
claims.quote: Their discovery facilitated medical research on the relation of blood cholesterol levels to atherosclerosis

claims.text: לפי הקרימזון, אליאס קורי אמר שהתגלית השפיעה מאוד על פיתוח תרופות ושימשה רבות ברפואה לשליטה ברמות כולסטרול ובמחלות מחזור הדם.
claims.quote: Emery Professor of Organic Chemistry Elias J. Corey said their discovery had a great effect on future drug development, and was used widely in medicine to control cholesterol levels and diseases of the circulatory system.

claims.text: לפי דקן בית הספר לבריאות הציבור, בארי בלום, אחד מהישגיו החשובים של בלוך היה פענוח מסלול הביוסינתזה של הכולסטרול.
claims.quote: one of Bloch's most important achievements was working out the pathway for the biosynthesis of cholesterol

claims.text: בלום כתב שזו הייתה אחת הבעיות המאתגרות ביותר שנלקחו אי פעם בביוכימיה עד אז.
claims.quote: It was one of the most challenging problems that had ever been undertaken in biochemistry at that point,

claims.text: הדקן ג'רמי נולס כינה את בלוך ביוכימאי מפוכח ומקשר בין כימיה לביוכימיה.
claims.quote: a marvelously perceptive biochemist and a wise, generous, and cultivated man who forged the connections between chemistry and biochemistry.

claims.text: בלוך זכה בין היתר בפרס פריצשה, בפרס המאה של נוטרדאם ובמדלית קרדנו.
claims.quote: Fritzsche Award (American Chemical Society, 1964), Centennial Science Award (University of Notre Dame, 1965), Cardano Medal (Lombardy Academy of Sciences, 1965)

claims.text: ב-1985 נעשה בלוך עמית החברה המלכותית.
claims.quote: In 1985, Bloch became a Fellow of the Royal Society.

claims.text: ב-1988 הוענק לבלוך מדליית המדע הלאומית של ארצות הברית.
claims.quote: In 1988, he was awarded the National Medal of Science.

claims.text: בלוך היה צנוע להפליא לעומת כישוריו והישגיו כמדען.
claims.quote: Konrad was remarkably humble for a scientist of his talents and accomplishments.

claims.text: לפי בלום, בלוך היה ענק מדעי אך תמיד אדם צנוע ונדיב ברעיונותיו ובחומריו המדעיים.
claims.quote: As much of a giant as he was scientifically, he was always a modest person, very generous with his thoughts and his scientific materials,

claims.text: בלוך פרש מעבודת הוראה במשרה מלאה בגיל 70 ב-1982, אך נשאר פעיל.
claims.quote: Bloch retired from full-time faculty work at age 70 in 1982, but remained quite active.

claims.text: בלוך כתב ספרים, ביניהם אוסף החיבורים "בלונדיניות בציורים ונציאניים, הארמדיל תשוע-הפסים וחיבורים אחרים בביוכימיה" (1994).
claims.quote: He wrote several books, including Blondes in Venetian Paintings, the Nine-Banded Armadillo, and Other Essays in Biochemistry (1994).

claims.text: בלוך מת ב-15 באוקטובר בקליניקת להיי בברלינגטון, מסצ'וסטס.
claims.quote: Konrad Emil Bloch, who won the Nobel Prize in Medicine or Physiology in 1964, died Sunday, Oct. 15, at Lahey Clinic in Burlington, Mass.

claims.text: בלוך אמר לטיים שמדובר ברצף מורכב להפליא של כ-36 תגובות ביוכימיות.
claims.quote: This is a fantastically complex sequence of approximately 36 biochemical reactions.

claims.text: בלוך אמר בחיוך שאולי יתברר שיש 39 תגובות, אך חששו שהרמז לא יובן לצעירים.
claims.quote: it may turn out that there are 39, but we were afraid this might be lost on the younger generation.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה לביוגרפיה עולמית, בלוך קיבל את הדוקטורט בביוכימיה ב-1938, בבית הספר לרפואה של אוניברסיטת קולומביה.
claims.quote: he earned his Ph.D. in biochemistry in 1938

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה לביוגרפיה עולמית, בלוך נעשה פרופסור חבר באוניברסיטת שיקגו ב-1948 ופרופסור מן המניין ב-1950.
claims.quote: becoming an associate professor in 1948 and a full professor in 1950
